passage:
Week one of October. Mohit's badminton coach, Sudha ma'am, filmed his smash again. Same speed on the tracker as in August. He had practised every morning. He stared at the number and thought, maybe this is it. Maybe this is my limit.
Week four. Still the same number. Mohit started leaving practice early, dragging his racket along the court floor. "I'm not improving, ma'am. I'm just not built for this."
Sudha ma'am said nothing. She pulled up two videos side by side, August and today. "Look at your feet." In August he had been flat-footed, lunging late. Now he was on his toes, arriving early under the shuttle.
Week six. In a practice match, Mohit returned three smashes he would have missed in the summer, without even thinking. The smash number hadn't changed. But on the bus home he replayed the rally and realised he had been getting better all along, just not where he was looking.

qa.q: What did Sudha ma'am tell Mohit to look at in the videos?
Why did Mohit think he had hit his limit in October?
qa.a: His smash speed showed the same number as in August despite daily practice, so he read no visible change as no progress at all.

qa.q: What did Sudha ma'am do that helped Mohit through the plateau?
qa.a: She put his August and current videos side by side to show hidden progress in his footwork, instead of arguing with him.

qa.q: What might Sudha ma'am have been thinking when Mohit said he wasn't built for this?
qa.a: She likely knew his footwork had improved and chose to show him rather than tell him, trusting the evidence to change his mind.

grounding: Shows a teenager on a badminton plateau who suspects he has reached his limit while his footwork has quietly improved.

passage:
Trisha, you're sulking because your Kathak footwork feels stuck? Sit. Let your Ojas Tauji tell you about a typewriter.
When I was fifteen, in Kanpur, Babuji sent me to Sharma-ji's typing institute so I could get a clerk's job one day. In the first month I went from nothing to twenty-five words a minute. I thought I'd be a champion by summer. Then I reached thirty, and there I stayed. Two whole months. Thirty, thirty, thirty.
I told Babuji I had no talent for it and wanted to stop. Sharma-ji, a strict old man, pulled out my test sheets from the first month and from the last week. Yes, my speed was the same. But my errors had fallen from fourteen a page to two. "Your hands learned something your stopwatch couldn't see," he said.
The next month I jumped to forty.
So, beta, your feet are learning something too. You just can't see it yet.

qa.q: What speed did Ojas get stuck at for two months?
Why did Ojas tell Babuji he had no talent for typing?
qa.a: His speed stayed at thirty for two months, so he felt discouraged and believed he had reached his limit.

qa.q: How did Sharma-ji reveal the hidden progress, and what could Trisha try?
qa.a: He compared early and recent test sheets, showing errors had fallen from fourteen a page to two; Trisha could compare old and new Kathak recordings to spot hidden gains in the footwork.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel hearing Tauji's typewriter story?
qa.a: Trisha may feel less alone and more hopeful that the stuck footwork is still improving under the surface.

grounding: Illustrates, through an uncle's memory of a typing plateau, how progress can continue beneath the surface when no visible change shows.
